title: Turnkey, EPC or Contractor-Managed: Which Delivery Model Fits Your Project
excerpt: Before a client decides who builds their project, they have to decide how it will be built — specifically, how many agencies they will appoint and who…
content:
Before a client decides who builds their project, they have to decide how it will be built — specifically, how many agencies they will appoint and who carries responsibility for the gaps between them.

This decision gets less attention than contractor selection, and it has comparable consequences. It determines who carries which risk, how much cost certainty you have, how much of your own time the project will take, and what happens when something goes wrong between two parties.

There are three main models. None is universally better.

Contractor-managed: you appoint separately, you coordinate

In this model the client appoints the architect, the structural consultant, the civil contractor, the MEP contractor, the facade contractor and the interiors contractor separately, and manages the relationships between them — directly or through a project management consultant.

What you gain. Direct control over each appointment, the ability to select a specialist for each package, visibility of each party’s rate rather than a single bundled figure, and flexibility to change scope within a package without renegotiating the whole project.

What it costs you. Every interface between agencies becomes your responsibility. The MEP contractor arrives to find a slab poured without sleeves; the facade contractor cannot start because of a structural tolerance issue; the interiors contractor waits on services that wait on something else. Each party will have planned its own work competently. Nobody owns the gaps — except you.

It also demands real in-house capacity. Someone on the client side needs the technical knowledge to coordinate drawings, the authority to make decisions quickly, and the time to run the project. Where that capacity genuinely exists, this model works well and can be the most cost-effective. Where it does not, the savings on paper are usually consumed by delay.

Turnkey: one contractor, one defined scope, one price

A turnkey contract gives a single contractor responsibility for delivering a defined scope for a fixed price. The client provides the design; the contractor builds everything in the scope and hands over a completed facility.

What you gain. Cost certainty from the outset, since quantity risk sits with the contractor. One point of responsibility for delivery. Substantially less client-side management time. And interface problems between trades become the contractor’s problem rather than yours.

What it requires. A properly defined scope before the contract is signed. This is the condition most often underestimated. A turnkey contract prices what is in the documents — every ambiguity becomes a variation claim, and a loosely defined turnkey contract delivers neither cost certainty nor goodwill.

The practical test: if your drawings and specifications are complete enough that a competent contractor could price them without asking you a series of clarifying questions, turnkey will work. If they are not, fix that before tendering rather than after.

EPC: engineering, procurement and construction under one contract

An EPC contract extends the turnkey model backwards to include design. The contractor takes a performance requirement — what the facility must do — and delivers engineering, procurement and construction against it.

What you gain. A single point of accountability from design through commissioning. No gap between designer and builder, which removes a common source of dispute, since the party doing the design is the party who has to build it. Faster start, because detailed design and early construction can overlap. And on complex industrial facilities, the contractor carries responsibility for whether the completed plant performs, not just whether it matches a drawing.

What it requires. A clear performance specification. Instead of telling the contractor what to build, you are telling them what it must achieve — throughput, capacity, compliance, operating parameters. Writing that well requires its own expertise, and a vague performance specification produces the same problems as a vague turnkey scope.

You also give up some design control. If the appearance and detail of every element matters to you, EPC may frustrate that. For an industrial facility where function governs, it rarely does.

Comparing them directly

Four questions separate the three models:

  • Who carries quantity risk? Contractor-managed: the client. Turnkey and EPC: the contractor.
  • Who owns the interfaces? Contractor-managed: the client. Turnkey and EPC: the contractor.
  • How much client-side capacity is needed? Contractor-managed: substantial. Turnkey: moderate. EPC: least.
  • How complete must the design be at tender? Contractor-managed: can evolve. Turnkey: complete. EPC: performance requirements complete, detailed design not needed.

There is a reasonable heuristic here. The less technical capacity you have in-house, and the more your project depends on complex interfaces between systems, the more single-point accountability is worth paying for. The more capacity you have, and the simpler the building, the more a separated approach can save.

On the cost comparison

Single-point models usually show a higher headline figure, because the contractor is pricing risk the client would otherwise carry. That premium is sometimes described as inefficiency. Often it is not.

The honest comparison includes the cost of client-side management time, the cost of delays caused by interface failures, the cost of variations arising from coordination gaps, and the cost of disputes between agencies where responsibility is unclear. These rarely appear in a tender comparison and they are real.

That said, the premium is not always justified. On a simple building where the client has genuine in-house capability, a separated approach can be materially cheaper with no meaningful increase in risk. The decision should be made on your actual situation rather than on a general preference for one model.

Choosing

Three questions, answered honestly:

  • Do we have someone who can run this project full time, with the technical knowledge to coordinate it? If not, a separated model will cost more than it appears to.
  • Is our design complete? If yes, turnkey is available. If only the performance requirements are settled, EPC is the fit.
  • How complex are the interfaces? The more systems that have to work together, the more single-point accountability is worth.

Whichever model you choose, the questions in our guide on “choosing a contractor” still apply. The delivery model determines how risk is allocated. It does not compensate for appointing the wrong firm.

At BlueWing, we work with clients on turnkey construction and EPC contracts across industrial, commercial and institutional projects, and we are equally willing to say when a separated approach would serve a client better.

Deciding how to structure an upcoming project? Talk to our team. We will give you an honest view of which model fits your situation — including when it is not one of ours.

faqs.question: What is the difference between turnkey and EPC?
faqs.answer: A turnkey contractor builds a defined scope for a fixed price, working to a design the client provides. An EPC contractor also carries out engineering and procurement, working to a performance specification rather than a completed design, and is accountable for whether the finished facility performs.

faqs.question: Is EPC more expensive than appointing contractors separately?
faqs.answer: The headline figure is usually higher, because the contractor prices risk the client would otherwise carry. The honest comparison includes client-side management time, interface delays and coordination variations, which rarely appear in a tender comparison.

faqs.question: When should a client choose a turnkey contract?
faqs.answer: When the design is complete enough to be priced without a series of clarifying questions, and when cost certainty matters more than flexibility to change scope during construction.

faqs.question: What is single-point accountability and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: It means one party is responsible for the whole delivery, including the interfaces between trades. It matters because interface failures between separately appointed agencies are one of the most common causes of construction delay, and in a separated model those gaps belong to the client.

faqs.question: Can a project change the delivery model partway through?
faqs.answer: Rarely without significant cost. The model affects how the design is developed, how the contract is written and how risk is priced, so it should be settled before tender rather than revisited during construction.

metaDescription: How the three main construction delivery models compare on risk, cost certainty and the in-house capacity each one demands from the client.

title: Educational Campus Construction: Building Around the Academic Calendar
excerpt: Most construction deadlines are negotiable under pressure. A campus deadline is not.If a new academic block is not ready when the session begins, the…
content:
Most construction deadlines are negotiable under pressure. A campus deadline is not.

If a new academic block is not ready when the session begins, the institution has students with nowhere to sit. There is no equivalent of phased occupancy or a short extension — the date is set by the academic calendar, it was published months in advance, and it does not move because a contractor is behind.

That single constraint shapes everything about how an education project should be planned.

The vacation window governs the programme

Work on an operating campus falls into two categories: what can be done while students are present, and what cannot.

Anything disruptive — demolition, structural work adjacent to occupied blocks, major services shutdowns, heavy material movement through campus — generally has to happen during vacation. That window is fixed, usually short, and if it is missed the work waits until the next one.

The planning implication is straightforward but frequently missed. Project sequencing should be built backwards from the vacation windows rather than forwards from the start date. Identify what must happen in each window, confirm that it fits, and only then set the overall programme. A sequence planned forwards will usually arrive at a vacation window with the wrong activity ready.

It also means long-lead procurement matters more here than on most project types. A material with a three-month lead time ordered late does not simply delay the work by three months — it can push an activity past a vacation window and delay it by six.

Working safely with students on site

A campus under construction is a site with several thousand untrained people on it, many of them young, none of them under the contractor’s supervision. This is a materially different safety proposition from a closed site.

What it requires in practice:

  • Hard physical separation between construction and campus areas — solid hoarding rather than tape or mesh, with no informal routes through the work area
  • Separate vehicle access for construction traffic, kept away from student movement routes entirely
  • Material movement scheduled outside class change times, when corridors and paths are busiest
  • Overhead protection where any work takes place above or beside a route in use
  • Noise management around examination periods, which in practice often means stopping certain activities altogether

The examination point deserves emphasis because it is the one most often overlooked at planning stage. Examination periods are fixed, they are non-negotiable, and noisy work during them will be stopped. Build them into the programme at the outset rather than discovering them in week twenty.

Different buildings, different demands

A campus is not one building type. The requirements vary sharply by facility, and each carries its own risk to the programme.

Laboratories are the most services-intensive buildings on a campus — fume extraction, gas lines, specialised drainage, power redundancy and bench services. They need design coordination closer to a healthcare project than to a classroom block, and the services often govern the structural sequence.

Auditoriums and lecture theatres bring long structural spans, raked floors, acoustic requirements and significant AV and HVAC provision. The span requirement in particular may push the structural solution in a different direction from the rest of the campus.

Hostels are highly repetitive, which makes them well suited to precast construction or system formwork. They also carry heavy plumbing and sanitary loads, and a fixed occupancy date that is usually the same as the session start.

Classroom and administrative blocks are closest to conventional commercial work, and are usually where programme recovery is possible if it is needed elsewhere.

Planning a campus as a single uniform project underestimates the laboratory and auditorium elements, which are where the programme risk concentrates.

Expansion is the normal condition

Very few campus projects are greenfield. Most are additions to a campus that has grown over years, and that carries specific implications.

Existing services need tracing before excavation, since campus utility records are frequently incomplete or out of date. New buildings connect into existing water, power and drainage networks that may already be at capacity. Architectural consistency with existing buildings is often a requirement rather than a preference. And the new structure has to work with circulation patterns that already exist — a building that is correct in isolation but awkward to reach is a poor outcome.

A practical recommendation: survey and trace existing services before finalising the foundation design, not after excavation starts. Unmarked services discovered mid-excavation are a common source of delay on campus projects specifically, because the records are so often unreliable.

Planning an education project

Five things worth settling early:

  • Fix the handover date to the academic session, then plan backwards from it rather than forwards from the start
  • Map the vacation windows across the full project duration and assign the disruptive work to them
  • Identify long-lead items early — on a campus project, a missed lead time can cost a whole vacation window
  • Agree the safety interface with the institution in writing, covering separation, access routes and restricted periods
  • Survey existing services before the foundation design is finalised

At BlueWing, we deliver institutional projects on a turnkey construction basis, and the projects we have delivered include educational work for clients including Parul University. Our precast division also supports repetitive building types such as hostel blocks where programme certainty matters.

Planning a campus building or expansion? Talk to our team early — on an education project, the sequencing decisions made before work starts matter more than almost anything that happens afterwards.

faqs.question: Can construction continue while a campus is operational?
faqs.answer: Yes, and most campus projects are executed this way. It requires hard physical separation from student areas, separate construction vehicle access, material movement scheduled outside class change times, and restrictions around examination periods.

faqs.question: How is a campus project programmed around the academic calendar?
faqs.answer: By planning backwards from the session start rather than forwards from the project start. Disruptive activities are assigned to vacation windows, which are fixed and usually short, and the rest of the sequence is built around them.

faqs.question: Which campus buildings are most complex to construct?
faqs.answer: Laboratories, because of fume extraction, gas lines, specialised drainage and power redundancy, and auditoriums, because of long structural spans, raked floors and acoustic requirements. Hostels and classroom blocks are more straightforward.

faqs.question: Is precast suitable for campus buildings?
faqs.answer: It suits highly repetitive buildings such as hostel blocks particularly well, where identical units allow mould cost to be spread and the programme benefit is real. It suits laboratories and auditoriums less well, where elements vary.

faqs.question: What delays campus construction most often?
faqs.answer: Missing a vacation window, usually because of a long-lead item ordered late or a sequencing decision made forwards rather than backwards from the session date. Unmarked existing services discovered during excavation are the second most common cause.

metaDescription: Why the academic session governs an education project — phasing around term dates, working safely with students present, and planning laboratory and hostel work.

title: Hospital Construction: What Makes It Different from a Commercial Building
excerpt: A hospital looks like a commercial building. It is not built like one.The structure may be conventional RCC, the floor plates may look similar to an office,…
content:
A hospital looks like a commercial building. It is not built like one.

The structure may be conventional RCC, the floor plates may look similar to an office, and the external envelope may be comparable. But almost everything that governs the programme, the cost and the risk is different — and clients who approach a healthcare project with commercial-building assumptions usually discover this partway through.

This article sets out the five areas where hospital construction genuinely diverges, and what each one means for planning a project.

1. Regulatory compliance is a design input, not a certificate at the end

A commercial building satisfies building regulations and fire safety requirements. A hospital satisfies those, and then a further layer of healthcare-specific requirements that affect the plan itself.

Accreditation standards, state health department licensing, biomedical waste rules, radiation safety approvals for imaging equipment, and fire safety provisions applied to a building where occupants cannot evacuate themselves — these shape corridor widths, door sizes, the relationship between departments, the separation of clean and contaminated routes, and the location of services.

The practical consequence: a hospital plan cannot be finalised and then checked for compliance. Compliance determines the plan. A layout that is efficient from a space-planning perspective may be unworkable once movement separation and licensing requirements are applied, and discovering that after the structure is built is extremely expensive.

Engage the compliance position at concept stage, with input from someone who has taken a healthcare facility through accreditation rather than from the general building code alone.

2. The services package dominates the project

On a commercial building, MEP services are a significant part of the project. On a hospital, they are the project, with a structure built around them.

Healthcare facilities carry systems that commercial buildings do not have at all:

  • Medical gas pipeline systems — oxygen, nitrous oxide, medical air and vacuum, distributed to defined outlet points with alarm and manifold arrangements
  • Specialised HVAC — operating theatres, intensive care units and isolation rooms require controlled air change rates, filtration, and defined pressure relationships between adjacent spaces
  • Redundant power — critical areas cannot lose supply, which means generator capacity, UPS provision and distribution designed so that a single failure does not take down a theatre
  • Radiation shielding — lead lining or high-density concrete to X-ray, CT and radiotherapy areas, with thickness determined by a radiation physicist rather than by a standard detail
  • Separated waste routes — biomedical waste handled apart from general waste from the point of generation

What this means for the programme: services coordination has to be resolved before the structure is poured, not alongside it. A slab penetration missed at the design stage becomes a core-cut through a structural element later, which is both expensive and sometimes refused by the structural consultant. On a hospital project, the services drawings govern the structural sequence more than the other way round.

3. Infection control applies during construction, not only after

This is the area most often underestimated, and it applies specifically to projects on an operational hospital site.

Construction generates dust. In a healthcare environment, airborne particulate carries a genuine risk to immunocompromised patients, and a construction activity next to an occupied ward is a clinical risk rather than a nuisance.

Managing it means sealed hoardings rather than open barriers, negative pressure within the work area so air does not flow from the construction zone toward patient areas, defined material and debris routes that do not pass through clinical zones, separate access and welfare arrangements for the construction workforce, and scheduled works for noisy or disruptive activities.

This is not a safety formality that can be adjusted later. Hospital management will stop work if it is not being managed properly, and a stoppage of this kind carries both programme and reputational cost. It needs to be priced and planned from the outset.

4. The hospital usually keeps running

A commercial project typically hands over a completed building. A hospital project, more often than not, is an extension or upgrade to a facility that continues to treat patients throughout.

That changes almost every assumption:

  • Work is phased rather than continuous, with each phase handed over before the next begins
  • Services must be maintained to existing areas while being modified — a power or medical gas shutdown has to be planned, approved and executed in a defined window
  • Access routes for ambulances, patients, staff and supplies cannot be obstructed at any point
  • Noise and vibration are restricted during clinical hours, which compresses the available working day
  • Each phase requires clearance before handover — a clinical area cannot be occupied until it meets the standard

Programme implications are significant. The same scope of work on a live hospital site will take considerably longer than on a greenfield plot, and a programme that does not reflect this is not realistic. It is better to establish that at the outset than to explain it in month eight.

5. Commissioning is a stage in its own right

On a commercial building, commissioning is largely a matter of testing systems and handing over. On a hospital, it is a formal process with clinical consequences.

Medical gas systems require purity and pressure testing with documented certification. Operating theatre air handling requires validation of air change rates, filter integrity and pressure differentials. Electrical systems need load testing with changeover verification. Radiation areas require survey and clearance before equipment is used.

All of this takes time, and none of it can be compressed, because the certification is what allows the facility to open. Building this period into the programme realistically is one of the clearest signs of a contractor who has done healthcare work before.

What to look for in a contractor

Four questions worth asking directly:

  • Which healthcare projects have you completed, and may we speak to those clients?
  • Have you worked on a live hospital site, and how did you manage infection control and phasing?
  • Do you execute medical gas and specialised HVAC in-house, or subcontract it? Either is acceptable — not knowing which is not.
  • How do you programme commissioning, and what did it actually take on your last healthcare project?

A contractor with healthcare experience will answer these immediately and in detail. One without will answer in general terms, and that difference tells you what you need to know.

At BlueWing, we deliver institutional and specialised projects on a turnkey or EPC basis as a construction contractor in Ahmedabad, with single-point accountability across structure, services and commissioning — which on a healthcare project is where most of the interface risk sits.

Planning a hospital project or an extension to an existing facility? Talk to our team. We will give you a realistic view of the programme, including the parts that commercial-building assumptions tend to miss.

faqs.question: How is hospital construction different from commercial construction?
faqs.answer: The structure may be similar, but healthcare-specific regulation shapes the plan itself, the services package is far larger and more complex, infection control applies during construction, work is usually phased around an operating facility, and commissioning is a formal certified process rather than a handover step.

faqs.question: How long does hospital construction take?
faqs.answer: Considerably longer than a commercial building of the same area, particularly on a live site where work is phased and working hours are restricted. Commissioning also takes meaningful time and cannot be compressed, since certification is what allows the facility to open.

faqs.question: What is the most commonly underestimated part of a hospital project?
faqs.answer: Infection control during construction on an operational site, and the time required for commissioning. Both are frequently treated as minor items at tender stage and both have real programme and cost consequences.

faqs.question: Can a hospital stay operational during construction?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and most healthcare projects are executed this way. It requires phased handover, sealed and pressure-controlled work areas, planned services shutdowns, protected access routes for patients and ambulances, and restricted working hours during clinical periods.

faqs.question: What should I check before appointing a hospital contractor?
faqs.answer: Completed healthcare projects with contactable references, experience of working on a live hospital site, whether medical gas and specialised HVAC are executed in-house or subcontracted, and how they programme commissioning.

seoTitle: Hospital Construction: How It Differs from Commercial Building
metaDescription: Regulatory compliance, infection control, medical gas and HVAC, and phased construction on a live hospital site — what makes healthcare projects different.

title: Basement Construction in Ahmedabad: What to Know Before You Start
excerpt: A basement is the most expensive floor in a building per square foot, and the one where problems are hardest to fix afterwards. Everything above ground can…
content:
A basement is the most expensive floor in a building per square foot, and the one where problems are hardest to fix afterwards. Everything above ground can be adjusted. A basement that leaks, or that had to be redesigned mid-excavation, stays expensive for the life of the building.

Most of what determines whether a basement goes well is decided before excavation begins — in the site investigation, the retention design and the waterproofing specification.

This article covers what matters specifically in Ahmedabad and across Gujarat: ground conditions, water, the approval position, the retention options, and what actually drives cost.

Ground conditions in and around Ahmedabad

Large parts of Gujarat sit on expansive clay soils, and this affects basement work more than most people expect.

Expansive clay swells when it takes on water and shrinks when it dries. The practical consequence is that ground behaviour changes seasonally. A retention design calculated against dry-season soil parameters can behave differently in August. Lateral earth pressures on a basement wall are not a fixed number across the year.

Ground conditions also vary considerably across the city. Sites near the river, in the older western areas, and on the eastern industrial belt can present quite different profiles. Neighbouring plots are not a reliable guide.

What this means practically: a proper geotechnical investigation is not optional, and it must extend meaningfully below the proposed excavation level. Boreholes stopped at basement formation level tell you nothing about what sits beneath the foundation — which is exactly where base heave and settlement problems originate.

Most basement disputes we see trace back to ground conditions that were not adequately established beforehand. The investigation is a small cost against the risk it removes.

Water

Groundwater is the second defining factor, and it varies both across the region and seasonally within it.

An investigation carried out in April may record a water table well below the proposed formation level. The same site in August may be quite different. If the design was based on the April reading, the excavation meets conditions nobody planned for.

Water affects a basement in three ways:

  • During excavation: Water flowing toward the excavation softens the face and can cause instability. This is the most common cause of serious excavation incidents.
  • During construction: Dewatering has to be maintained continuously, not treated as a one-time operation at the start. Placing reinforcement and concrete in a partly flooded excavation produces defects that surface later.
  • Permanently: The completed basement sits below the water table and is subject to hydrostatic pressure for the life of the building. This is a waterproofing and structural design question, not a construction one.

Water strategy should be settled before excavation begins, not resolved during it. On our own basement works on a waterlogged site, the sequence of dewatering, foundation-bed preparation and rubble soling was established before the first excavation, which is what allowed the RCC foundation to be placed on stable ground rather than on something still moving.

The approval position

Basement construction in Ahmedabad is governed by the Comprehensive General Development Control Regulations and administered locally by AUDA or the Municipal Corporation depending on where the site falls.

Approval requirements cover permissible basement extent relative to the plot, setback and margin conditions, permitted basement uses, ventilation and access requirements, and fire safety provisions including escape routes.

Two practical points:

  • Approvals affect the design, not just the paperwork. Permissible basement footprint and setback requirements shape the retention design and the excavation sequence. Resolving these late means redesigning work already priced.
  • Multi-level basements attract more scrutiny. Fire safety, ventilation and access requirements become more demanding with depth, and these are easier to design in than to retrofit.

Engage the approval position at concept stage. It is a design input, not a step at the end.

Choosing the retention system

The retention system holds back soil and water while you excavate. It is the single most consequential decision in a basement project.

Open cut with battered slopes is simplest and cheapest, but needs spare land around the excavation. On an urban plot built close to the boundary, it is unavailable.

Sheet piling installs quickly and the sections are recoverable, but driving causes vibration that limits use next to existing buildings, and a permanent basement wall is still required inside it.

Contiguous or secant piling forms a wall from bored piles. Contiguous suits sites above the water table; secant piles interlock to resist water and can be structural. On single and double basements this is often the right commercial answer.

A diaphragm wall is constructed in panels from ground level before excavation begins, giving a continuous reinforced concrete wall that serves as both the temporary retention and the permanent basement wall. Where a diaphragm wall earns its cost is on deep basements, high water tables, and plots where existing buildings sit close to the boundary — because the ground next to that boundary is never left unsupported.

Choosing between them comes down to depth, water, proximity to neighbours and site space. A single basement in reasonable ground with room around it does not need a diaphragm wall. A three-level basement below the water table on a boundary-to-boundary plot almost certainly does.

Waterproofing

Waterproofing is where basements fail, and it is routinely under-specified.

The distinction that matters is between tanking — a membrane barrier applied to keep water out — and structural waterproofing, where the concrete itself is designed to resist water penetration, usually combined with waterstops at construction joints.

For basements below the water table, structural waterproofing with proper joint detailing is generally more reliable than relying on a membrane alone. A membrane is only as good as its continuity, and continuity is difficult to guarantee across a complex basement geometry with penetrations.

The failure points are consistent: construction joints, penetrations for services, and the junction between wall and base slab. These need detailing at design stage and inspection during execution. A basement that leaks almost never leaks through the middle of a wall.

One more point worth stating plainly: waterproofing cannot be inspected after completion. It has to be verified while it is being built.

What drives cost

Basement cost per square foot runs well above superstructure cost, and the gap widens with depth. The main drivers:

  • Depth: The relationship is not linear. Each additional level increases retention requirements, dewatering duration and structural demands more than proportionally.
  • Water table position: A basement above the water table is a substantially different proposition from one below it.
  • Retention system: Often the largest single line item on a deep basement.
  • Soil conditions: Poor or variable ground increases both retention cost and foundation cost.
  • Site constraints: Restricted access, limited working space and proximity to neighbours all slow execution and raise cost.
  • Excavated material disposal: Significant on deep basements, and frequently underestimated at budget stage.

What reduces cost: settling the design early so the retention system is right first time, a proper site investigation that removes surprises, and a realistic programme. Compressed basement programmes tend to cost more, not less, because the sequence does not compress well.

Before you start

Five things to have in place:

  • A geotechnical investigation extending well below formation level, ideally with seasonal water table data.
  • The approval position confirmed — permissible extent, setbacks, fire and ventilation requirements.
  • The retention system selected at design stage, with the structural consultant.
  • A water strategy covering construction dewatering and permanent waterproofing.
  • A contractor with genuine basement experience, not a general contractor subcontracting the specialist work without telling you.

On the last point: ask directly whether basement and retention work is executed in-house or subcontracted. Both are acceptable. Not knowing which you are getting is not.

At BlueWing, we execute basement and retention work as a construction contractor in Ahmedabad across commercial, industrial and residential projects, with diaphragm wall construction carried out in-house through our subsidiary Sygnific Infra.

Planning a basement?

Talk to our team with your site location and depth requirement. We will tell you what the ground conditions are likely to demand — and what they are likely to cost.

faqs.question: How much does basement construction cost in Ahmedabad?
faqs.answer: Cost per square foot runs well above superstructure rates and depends heavily on depth, water table position, soil conditions and retention system. Depth is the dominant variable, and the relationship is not linear — each additional level costs more than the one above it.

faqs.question: Do I need approval for a basement in Ahmedabad?
faqs.answer: Yes. Basement construction is governed by the Comprehensive General Development Control Regulations, administered by AUDA or the Municipal Corporation depending on location. Requirements cover permissible extent, setbacks, ventilation, access and fire safety.

faqs.question: How deep can a basement be built in Ahmedabad?
faqs.answer: Technically, multi-level basements are achievable — diaphragm walls can be constructed to 45 metres. The practical limits are usually regulatory and commercial rather than technical.

faqs.question: Why do basements leak?
faqs.answer: Almost always at construction joints, service penetrations, or the wall-to-base-slab junction. Rarely through the middle of a wall. These points need detailing at design stage and inspection during construction, since waterproofing cannot be verified after completion.

faqs.question: Is a site investigation really necessary for a single basement?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ground conditions vary significantly across Ahmedabad, and neighbouring plots are not a reliable guide. The investigation cost is small against the risk of discovering conditions mid-excavation.

seoTitle: Basement Construction in Ahmedabad: What to Know First
metaDescription: Soil conditions, water table, retention systems, waterproofing and cost drivers — a practical guide to basement construction in Ahmedabad and Gujarat.

title: What Actually Delays Construction Projects
excerpt: Most construction delays are blamed on the contractor. Some of them are the contractor’s fault.But when a project runs six months late, the cause is rarely…
content:
Most construction delays are blamed on the contractor. Some of them are the contractor’s fault.

But when a project runs six months late, the cause is rarely a single failure. It is usually a sequence of smaller delays, most of which were predictable, and several of which originated well before the contractor was appointed.

This article sets out what actually causes delay, roughly in order of how much time it accounts for — and, more usefully, which causes can be removed in advance and which can only be managed.

1. Design that was never finished

The largest single cause of delay is starting construction on a design that is not complete.

It happens for understandable reasons. The client wants to start, approvals are in hand, the foundation design is settled, and the reasoning is that upper floor details can be resolved while the substructure is built.

Sometimes that works. Often it does not, because design decisions are connected. A change to a service route affects slab penetrations. A revised layout affects column positions. A change made in month four turns out to contradict something built in month two.

The cost is not only the direct rework. It is the decision-waiting time — days where a crew has nothing to do because a detail has not been issued, which do not appear as a delay event anywhere but accumulate steadily.

What removes it: freezing the structural design before construction starts, and resolving services coordination before the slab it affects is poured. This is unglamorous and it is the highest-return thing a client can do.

2. Approvals

Approval timelines are treated as fixed inputs when they are largely variable, and they are frequently the cause of the first slippage in a programme.

Delay comes less often from the approving authority than from incomplete submissions, drawings that do not match regulations, revisions required after review, and the queue position a resubmission goes to.

Multi-level basements, industrial projects and buildings above certain heights attract additional scrutiny — fire safety, environmental clearance, and pollution control consent each carry their own timeline.

What removes it: engaging the approval position at design stage rather than after drawings are complete, and submitting complete applications first time. A resubmission usually costs more calendar time than the extra week spent getting the first one right.

3. Material lead times

Not all materials are available on demand, and the ones with long lead times are rarely on anyone’s critical path until they are.

Structural steel in specific sections, imported fittings, lifts and escalators, specialist facade systems, and large electrical equipment can carry lead times running to several months. Cement and aggregate rarely cause delay. The items that do are usually the ones ordered late because they are needed late.

The sequencing error is common: a lift with a four-month lead time ordered when the shaft is ready, rather than four months before.

What removes it: identifying long-lead items at the start of the project and placing orders against the programme rather than against site readiness.

4. Labour availability and the festival season

Labour availability in Gujarat is seasonal, and it is predictable enough that it should never be a surprise.

The most significant period is Navratri through Diwali. A substantial proportion of the workforce returns home, and many do not return immediately afterwards. Depending on the trade and the source region, a site can be operating at reduced strength for several weeks around the festival period, with a further ramp-up period after.

Monsoon has a different effect — work continues, but slows. Excavation, external work and concrete pours are all affected, and the overall rate of progress falls even on a well-managed site.

What removes it: planning around it rather than through it. Practically, that means scheduling labour-intensive activities outside the festival window, completing critical path items before the break rather than assuming they will continue through it, and building a realistic ramp-up period into the programme rather than assuming full strength returns on day one.

A programme that assumes uninterrupted full-strength working through October and November is not a programme. It is a hope.

5. Payment cycles

This one is rarely discussed openly and accounts for more delay than its visibility suggests.

Construction runs on working capital. A contractor who is not paid on time cannot pay suppliers on time, which affects material deliveries. They cannot pay labour on time, which affects retention of crews. And they will, reasonably, prioritise sites where payment is current.

Delayed certification has the same effect as delayed payment. A bill that sits unapproved for three weeks is a three-week working capital gap.

What removes it: a realistic payment schedule agreed at contract stage, certification turned around within the agreed period, and disputed items separated from undisputed ones so that a disagreement over one item does not hold up payment for the rest.

6. Contractor capacity

A contractor operating beyond capacity will deliver worse results than a smaller firm with room for your project.

The symptoms are recognisable: the project manager is running several sites and visits yours twice a week, key decisions wait for someone who is not available, and crews are moved between sites according to which client is complaining loudest.

This is worth checking before appointment rather than discovering afterwards. When choosing a contractor, ask what their current order book looks like and where your project would sit in their priorities. It is the question clients most often skip and most often regret.

7. Site conditions that were not investigated

Ground conditions that differ from what was assumed are a common source of delay, and they are usually discovered at the worst possible moment — after excavation has started.

Unexpected water, poor bearing capacity, buried obstructions and rock all require design changes mid-execution, which means redesign time, revised approvals in some cases, and reprogramming.

What removes it: a proper geotechnical investigation extending below the proposed foundation level. It is a small cost against the risk.

8. Coordination between agencies

On a project with separate civil, MEP, facade and interior contractors, the interfaces between them are where time is lost. Each agency plans its own work well. Nobody owns the gaps.

Typical failures: the MEP contractor arrives to find the slab poured without the required sleeves, the facade contractor cannot start because the structural frame has a tolerance issue, the interiors contractor waits on services that wait on something else.

What removes it: either genuine coordination management by the client or their consultant, or a turnkey or EPC basis contract where a single contractor carries responsibility for the interfaces. This is the main argument for single-point delivery, and it is worth more on complex projects than the headline cost comparison suggests.

What this means in practice

Of the eight causes above, five are largely settled before construction begins: design completeness, approvals, long-lead procurement, contractor selection and site investigation.

That is the useful conclusion. Most of the delay in a construction project is determined by decisions taken before anyone arrives on site. Once construction is underway, the scope for recovery is limited — you can manage delay, but removing it is much harder than preventing it.

The three that remain live during execution — labour seasonality, payment cycles and interface coordination — are all manageable with planning that most projects simply do not do.

A closing observation. When a programme is compressed at tender stage to satisfy a target date, without any change to scope or resources, the delay is being scheduled rather than avoided. It will appear later, and by then it will cost more to address. A programme that is realistic at the outset is the cheapest form of delay prevention available.

At BlueWing, we work with clients on a turnkey or EPC basis where single-point accountability removes the interface coordination problem entirely.

Planning a project and want a realistic view of the programme?

Talk to our team.

faqs.question: What is the most common cause of construction delay?
faqs.answer: Starting construction on an incomplete design. It generates both direct rework and a steady accumulation of decision-waiting time that rarely gets recorded as delay but adds up substantially.

faqs.question: How much does the festival season affect construction in Gujarat?
faqs.answer: Significantly. A substantial proportion of the workforce travels home around Navratri and Diwali, and return is staggered. Sites commonly run at reduced strength for several weeks, with a further ramp-up period afterwards.

faqs.question: Can construction delays be recovered?
faqs.answer: Partly, through resequencing, additional resources or overtime — all of which cost money. Prevention is substantially cheaper than recovery, which is why the decisions made before construction starts matter more than those made during it.

faqs.question: Who is responsible for delay in a construction contract?
faqs.answer: It depends on the cause and on the contract. Contractor-caused delay usually attracts liquidated damages; client-caused delay usually entitles the contractor to an extension of time and often to cost. Most real delays involve contributions from both sides, which is why a clear contract and proper records matter.

faqs.question: How can a client reduce the risk of delay?
faqs.answer: Freeze the design before starting, engage approvals at design stage, order long-lead items early, investigate the ground properly, and appoint a contractor with the capacity to prioritise your project.

title: Precast vs Conventional Construction: Cost and Time Compared
excerpt: Precast is often presented as the modern alternative to conventional construction — faster, cleaner, more consistent. Conventional construction is often…
content:
Precast is often presented as the modern alternative to conventional construction — faster, cleaner, more consistent. Conventional construction is often defended as more flexible and better understood.

Both positions are partly right, which is why the comparison is worth doing properly rather than settling by preference.

This article compares the two on the things that actually decide a project: cost, programme, quality, flexibility and risk. It also sets out the conditions under which each is the better answer.

What the two actually are


Conventional construction, also called cast-in-situ, forms the structure in position. Formwork is erected on site, reinforcement is fixed, concrete is poured, and the formwork is struck once the concrete has gained strength. Each element is built where it will stand.

Precast construction manufactures structural elements — columns, beams, slabs, wall panels, staircases — in a controlled factory environment. Elements are cured, transported to site, and assembled with cast-in-situ joints connecting them.

The important difference is not the concrete. It is where the work happens, and therefore what governs the programme. Conventional construction is limited by site conditions and curing time. Precast is limited by factory capacity, transport and crane availability.

Programme

This is where precast makes its strongest case.

In conventional construction, the floor cycle governs everything. Each floor requires formwork erection, reinforcement, pouring, curing and striking before the next can proceed. The cycle can be compressed with aluminium formwork systems and careful planning, but curing time sets a floor below which it cannot go.

Precast decouples manufacture from site work. Elements for upper floors can be produced while the foundation is still being built. Once erection begins, the site sequence becomes assembly rather than construction, and progress is measured in elements placed per day rather than floors per cycle.

Two practical consequences:

  • Weather dependency drops sharply. Monsoon has limited effect on factory production. On a conventional site, heavy rain stops pours, delays curing and slows every trade. For projects that must run through the monsoon, this is often the deciding argument.
  • But the design freeze comes much earlier. Precast requires complete structural design before manufacturing starts. On a conventional project, design details can still be resolved while the lower floors are built. On a precast project they cannot. Time saved on site is partly spent earlier in the programme.

Precast delivers its programme advantage where the structure is repetitive and the design can be frozen early. On a project where the client is still resolving layouts, that advantage largely disappears.

Cost

Cost comparison is where most discussions of precast go wrong, because the two systems distribute cost differently rather than one simply being cheaper.

Precast carries higher upfront cost. Moulds have to be fabricated, and that cost is fixed regardless of how many elements are produced from them. Transport is a real cost that conventional construction does not carry at all. Erection needs cranes of adequate capacity, and crane availability is a cost and a constraint.

Precast reduces cost elsewhere. Site labour requirement falls substantially. Formwork material and its repeated handling largely disappear. Material wastage is lower in a factory than on a site. Shorter site duration reduces preliminaries, supervision and site establishment costs. And on a commercial project, earlier completion means earlier revenue — which on a large development can outweigh the construction cost difference entirely.

The variable that decides it is repetition. Mould cost divided across twenty identical elements is a small figure. Divided across three, it is not. This is why precast performs well on repetitive residential, industrial and institutional buildings, and poorly on one-off structures with varied elements.

A note on quoted rates. Comparing a precast rate against a conventional rate directly is misleading, because the scope boundaries usually differ. Ask what is included in each: does the precast rate cover transport, erection, cranes and jointing? Does the conventional rate include formwork, or is that separate? Most apparent price gaps between the two disappear once the inclusions are aligned.

Quality

Factory production gives precast a genuine advantage in consistency.

Concrete is batched and cured under controlled conditions rather than in monsoon humidity or summer heat. Dimensional accuracy is higher, because elements are cast against steel moulds rather than site-assembled formwork. Finishes are more consistent, which reduces plaster and levelling work downstream. And elements are inspected before they leave the factory, so a defective element is rejected rather than built into the structure.

Conventional construction can achieve equivalent quality, but it depends more heavily on site supervision, workmanship and conditions on the day. The variability is higher.

The area where precast demands more attention is joints. A precast structure is only as good as the connections between its elements. Joint detailing, grouting and the cast-in-situ topping are the critical items, and they are where precast projects go wrong when they go wrong.

Flexibility

This is conventional construction’s clearest advantage.

Cast-in-situ construction accommodates change. A dimension can be adjusted, an opening added, a detail resolved on site. Irregular geometry is straightforward. Changes after work has begun are manageable and often cheap.

Precast does not accommodate change well. Once a mould is fabricated and elements are in production, a design change means new moulds, revised elements and disruption to a manufacturing sequence. Late changes on a precast project are expensive.

For projects with complex architectural geometry, or where the client’s requirements are still evolving, conventional construction remains the practical choice.

Site conditions

Precast imposes site requirements that are easy to overlook at the decision stage.

Elements arrive on trailers, so the site needs access suitable for long vehicle movements. There must be space to receive and stack elements before erection. Cranes of adequate capacity and reach are needed throughout erection. And the site layout must allow crane positioning to cover the building footprint.

On a tight urban plot with constrained access, these requirements can rule precast out regardless of its other merits. On an open industrial site, they are rarely a problem.

Which suits your project


Precast is likely the better choice where:

  • The structure is highly repetitive — similar floors, similar elements
  • Programme certainty matters more than flexibility
  • Design can be frozen before construction begins
  • The project must progress through the monsoon
  • The site has good access, space and crane capability
  • Volume is sufficient to spread mould cost

Conventional construction is likely better where:

  • The design is irregular or architecturally complex
  • Requirements are still being resolved
  • The plot is tight, with restricted access
  • The project is small, or elements vary widely
  • Local skilled labour is readily available and cost-competitive

A hybrid approach is often the right answer, and is frequently overlooked. Precast slabs or wall panels combined with a cast-in-situ frame can capture much of the programme advantage without demanding the full design freeze. This works particularly well on projects where part of the structure repeats and part does not.

The decision is made earlier than most people think

The most common mistake is treating this as a tender-stage question. By the time drawings are complete and priced, the structural design has usually been developed for one system, and switching is expensive.

The comparison belongs at concept stage, alongside the structural consultant. That is when programme, layout and cost can all still respond to the choice.

At BlueWing, we deliver both. Our precast construction division, Bhaarat Precast, manufactures and erects precast elements, while our turnkey construction projects are executed conventionally where that suits the project better. We have no commercial reason to push one over the other — which is the position you want a contractor in when asking this question.

Deciding between precast and conventional for an upcoming project?

Talk to our team — we will give you an honest assessment of which suits your programme, site and design.

faqs.question: Is precast construction cheaper than conventional?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. Precast has higher upfront costs in moulds, transport and cranes, but lower site labour, formwork and preliminaries. The deciding factor is repetition — the more identical elements, the better precast performs.

faqs.question: Is precast construction faster?
faqs.answer: On site, substantially. Elements are manufactured while site work proceeds, so the two happen in parallel. But precast requires the design to be frozen earlier, so total project duration from concept improves less than site duration suggests.

faqs.question: Is precast concrete as strong as cast-in-situ?
faqs.answer: Yes, and factory conditions often give more consistent strength. The critical element is joint detailing between precast units, which requires careful design and execution.

faqs.question: Can precast be used for high-rise buildings?
faqs.answer: Yes, commonly, particularly for repetitive residential towers. Crane capacity and site logistics become the governing constraints as height increases.

faqs.question: Does precast work during monsoon?
faqs.answer: Manufacture is largely unaffected, since it happens in a factory. Erection continues in most conditions, though crane operation stops during high winds. This weather independence is one of precast's strongest arguments in Gujarat.

title: Diaphragm Walls for Deep Basements: When to Specify One
excerpt: Deep basement construction is the stage of a project where the gap between a good decision and a poor one is widest. Above ground, a mistake usually costs…
content:
Deep basement construction is the stage of a project where the gap between a good decision and a poor one is widest. Above ground, a mistake usually costs money. Below ground, next to an existing building, it can cost a great deal more.

The retention system — the structure that holds back soil and water while you excavate — is the decision that governs this. It is often made late, treated as a contractor’s means and methods question, and priced against alternatives that are not really comparable.

This article sets out what actually governs safety during deep excavation, how the main retention systems compare, and the conditions under which a diaphragm wall is the right specification. It also covers where it is not.

What Actually Governs Safety in a Deep Excavation

Four things go wrong during deep basement work. Every retention system is really a way of managing them.

1. Face instability. Soil has limited ability to stand vertically. Beyond a certain depth — much shallower in saturated ground than in dry — an unsupported face will fail. This is the most common cause of serious excavation incidents, and it rarely gives much warning.

2. Water ingress and base heave. Where the excavation extends below the water table, water flows toward the excavation. This softens the face, can cause piping and erosion, and in some soil profiles produces base heave, where the excavation floor is pushed upward by water pressure beneath it.

3. Settlement of adjacent structures. Excavation removes lateral support from the ground next to it. That ground moves toward the excavation, and any building founded on it settles. Even small movements can crack a neighbouring structure — and the claim that follows is often larger than the excavation contract.

4. Vibration during installation. Some retention systems are installed by driving elements into the ground. That transmits vibration, which is a problem adjacent to older buildings or sensitive equipment.

A retention system is a means of controlling these four things. Which system suits your project depends on which of them are actually present.

Comparing the Main Retention Systems

Open-cut with battered slopes is the simplest and cheapest approach: excavate at a slope shallow enough to stand unsupported. It works only where there is spare land around the excavation and where the depth is modest. On an urban plot built to the boundary, it is not available at all.

Sheet piling uses interlocking steel sections driven into the ground. Fast to install, and the sections are recoverable. But installation vibration limits its use next to existing structures, penetration is difficult in dense or bouldery ground, and the sheets are temporary — a permanent basement wall is still required inside them.

Contiguous or secant piling forms a wall from a row of bored piles. Contiguous piles are spaced with gaps, so they suit sites above the water table. Secant piles interlock to give a water-resisting wall, and can be structural. This is a genuine competitor to a diaphragm wall on many sites, and on smaller or shallower basements it is often the better commercial answer.

Diaphragm walls are formed by excavating a trench in panels, holding the trench open with bentonite slurry, lowering a reinforcement cage, and placing concrete to displace the slurry. The result is a continuous reinforced concrete wall, installed before any bulk excavation begins.

Where the Diaphragm Wall Advantage Actually Lies

Four characteristics matter.

Depth. Diaphragm walls can be constructed considerably deeper than most alternatives — up to 45 metres in our own execution — while maintaining structural continuity and verticality control. Where a basement runs to three, four or more levels, this becomes the practical constraint that rules other systems out.

Water control. The wall is continuous, not an assembly of separate elements with joints between them. This gives a genuine cut-off, which matters where the excavation sits below the water table — and it is a significant part of the safety argument, since water ingress is what turns a stable excavation into an unstable one.

Proximity to existing structures. The wall is installed from ground level before excavation begins, so the ground next to the boundary is never left unsupported. Excavation happens inside a structure that already exists. This is the reason D-Wall dominates on congested urban plots.

No driving vibration. Panels are excavated, not driven. Adjacent to older buildings or sensitive facilities, this is often the deciding factor.

There is also a commercial argument that is frequently overlooked. A diaphragm wall is a permanent structural element — it serves as the basement retaining wall in the finished building. It replaces the permanent wall rather than sitting outside it. Compared against a temporary system plus a separate permanent wall, and against the plan area lost to a double-wall arrangement, the cost comparison often looks quite different from the headline rate.

Where a Diaphragm Wall Is Not the Right Answer

An honest assessment has to include this, and any contractor who will not give you one is not the contractor you want.

Shallow basements. For a single basement level in reasonable ground, a diaphragm wall is usually over-specified. Contiguous piling or an open cut will serve at lower cost.

Small plan areas. D-Wall carries significant setup cost — slurry plant, desanding equipment, grabs, cranes. Spread across a small wall area, the rate per square metre becomes uncompetitive.

Sites with no room for the plant. The slurry batching and treatment plant needs space and access for material movement. On a very tight site with poor access, this can be a genuine constraint.

Ground above the water table with no adjacency issues. If there is no water to cut off and no neighbouring structure to protect, the main advantages are not being used.

The right question is not “is D-Wall better.” It is “which of the four risks are present on this site, and which system addresses them at the lowest total cost.”

How a Diaphragm Wall Is Built

Understanding the sequence helps in evaluating a diaphragm wall contractor, because most of what determines quality is invisible on completion.

Guide walls are constructed first — two short parallel concrete walls at ground level that define the trench alignment and stabilise the upper soil during excavation. Their accuracy governs the accuracy of everything below.

Panel excavation proceeds using a grab or cutter, in discrete panels rather than continuously. The trench is kept filled with bentonite slurry throughout. The slurry exerts pressure against the trench walls, which is what holds them open.

Stop ends are placed at panel edges to form the joint profile against which the adjacent panel will be cast.

The reinforcement cage is lowered into the slurry-filled trench as a single assembly, with cover spacers to maintain position.

Concrete is placed by tremie, from the bottom upward, displacing the slurry as it rises. The tremie pipe must stay embedded in the concrete throughout — if it lifts clear, slurry becomes trapped in the pour and creates a defect that will not be visible until excavation exposes it.

Excavation and anchoring follow, with the wall supported by ground anchors or internal props as the dig advances.

The quality-critical points are slurry condition, verticality, cage position and tremie discipline. When you evaluate a contractor, ask what they record at each of these stages and ask to see the records from a live project. A firm that documents them properly will show you immediately.

The Gujarat Context

Two regional factors matter.

Large parts of Gujarat sit on expansive clay soils that swell when saturated and shrink when dry. This affects both the design of the retention system and the behaviour of the ground next to it, particularly across seasons. A retention design calculated on dry-season parameters can behave differently in August.

Groundwater levels also vary considerably across the region and seasonally within it. A site investigation carried out in one season may not represent the conditions the excavation will actually face — which is why we treat water control as a design input rather than a site problem to be solved later, and why basement works on a waterlogged site need the water strategy settled before excavation starts, not during it.

Making the Decision

Bring the retention system into the discussion early, at design stage rather than tender stage. It affects basement layout, structural design and programme, and by the time drawings are frozen the genuinely better options may already be closed off.

Have a proper site investigation done, extending below the proposed excavation level. Most retention system disputes trace back to ground conditions that were not adequately established beforehand.

And ask any contractor to make the case against their own recommendation. A firm that can explain when their preferred system would be the wrong choice is a firm that understands it.

At BlueWing, our subsidiary Sygnific Infra executes diaphragm wall construction to depths of 45 metres and thicknesses from 300 mm to 1200 mm, alongside our turnkey and EPC projects across Gujarat.

Planning a deep basement? Talk to our team with your site details and basement depth. We will tell you whether a diaphragm wall is the right solution — and if it is not, we will say so.

faqs.question: How deep can a diaphragm wall be constructed?
faqs.answer: Depths of 45 metres are achievable with appropriate equipment and verticality control. The practical limit on most building projects is set by the basement design rather than by the technique.

faqs.question: Is a diaphragm wall cheaper than secant piling?
faqs.answer: Not usually on a straight rate comparison. The comparison changes when you account for the diaphragm wall serving as the permanent basement wall, the plan area saved, and the reduced water-control cost during construction. On deep basements the total cost often favours D-Wall; on shallow ones it rarely does.

faqs.question: Can a diaphragm wall be built close to an existing building?
faqs.answer: Yes — this is its main advantage. The wall is installed from ground level before excavation, so the ground adjacent to the boundary is never left unsupported, and there is no driving vibration during installation.

faqs.question: What is bentonite slurry used for?
faqs.answer: It fills the trench during excavation and exerts pressure against the trench walls, holding them open until concrete is placed. Its density, viscosity and sand content are tested throughout, as slurry condition directly affects the quality of the finished panel.

faqs.question: Does a diaphragm wall stop water?
faqs.answer: It provides a continuous cut-off with no joints between separate elements, which substantially reduces ingress. It is usually combined with additional waterproofing measures depending on the intended basement use.
